Based on your description—specifically that it sucks fine (meaning the motor is running and airflow isn't blocked) but the brush stopped spinning and you smelled burning rubber—the issue is almost certainly a mechanical failure in the brush roll drive system.

Here’s what likely happened and how to fix it:

### 🔍 Most Likely Cause: Broken Drive Belt
The "burning rubber" smell is the classic sign of a drive belt slipping or snapping.
• The motor spins, but the belt that transfers power from the motor to the brush roll has either:
• Slipped off its pulleys.
• Stretched and worn out, causing it to slip (creating heat/smell) until it finally broke or lost grip.
• Snapped completely.

Since suction is still good, the main motor is fine—only the brush drive is affected.

---

### ✅ How to Fix It

#### 🛠️ Step-by-Step Diagnosis & Repair:
1. Unplug the vacuum. Safety first!
2. Remove the brush roll cover:
• Flip the vacuum upright so you can see the bottom where the brush rolls are.
• Look for screws or clips holding the plastic plate/cover over the brush roll. Remove them carefully.
3. Inspect the drive belt:
• You’ll see a small rubber loop (belt) connecting two pulleys: one on the motor shaft and one on the brush roll axle.
• If it’s broken or missing: Replace the belt. Find your vacuum model number (usually on a sticker under the dustbin or near the hose connection) and search online for "[Your Model] drive belt." They’re cheap ($5–$10).
• If it’s intact but loose/slipped off: Try to reseat it on both pulleys. If it’s stretched, cracked, or shiny/smooth (not grooved), replace it anyway—it won’t hold tension long-term.
4. Check for obstructions in the brush roll:
• While you’re there, remove any hair, string, or debris wrapped around the brush roll ends. This can cause binding and burn belts.
• Spin the brush roll by hand to ensure it moves freely.
5. Reassemble and test.

---

### ⚠️ Other Possible (But Less Likely) Causes:
• Brush roll bearings seized: If the brush roll doesn’t spin freely by hand even after removing debris, the bearings may be jammed. This would also cause belt burnout. You’d need to replace the brush roll assembly.
• Drive clutch/gearbox failure (rare in uprights): Some models have a gear mechanism instead of a direct belt. If yours has gears and they’re stripped, you’ll hear grinding or clicking. But the "burning rubber" smell strongly points to a belt.

---

### 💡 Pro Tip:
• Prevent future issues: Clean hair/debris from the brush roll every 1–2 months. Replace belts annually if you have pets or high-pile carpet.
• If your vacuum is under warranty: Contact the manufacturer before opening it, as self-repair may void coverage.

Great job diagnosing that! The shiny/melted edges on the belt pieces confirm that friction from the tangled debris caused overheating until the belt snapped. Since you’ve already cleared the hair/tassel and the brushbar spins freely, replacing the belt is your next step. Here’s how to proceed:

### ✅ Replacement Belt for Vax Air Stretch U85-AS-Be
1. Order a replacement belt:
   Search for "Vax U85 drive belt" or "Vax Air Stretch U85 brushroll belt". Ensure it matches your model (U85-AS-Be). These cost ~£5–£10 online.

2. Install the new belt:
• Remove the remaining broken belt pieces from the pulleys.
• Loop the new belt around the motor shaft first, then stretch it onto the brushroll axle. Ensure it’s seated snugly in both grooves.

3. Reassemble and test:
• Replace the brushbar cover and secure screws/clips.
• Plug in the vacuum and turn it on. The brush should spin smoothly without slipping or burning smells.

### 🔍 Pro Tips:
• Check pulleys: Ensure both motor and brushroll pulleys are clean and undamaged. If they’re worn, replace them too (though rare).
• Prevent future tangles: Use a brushbar guard or regularly clear debris to avoid recurrence.
